story: Long winters, short summers and a very relaxed attitude to sitting in hot rooms.
hints: Check the coffee. And the saunas.
Lots of trees, lots of headbanging.
why: Around three million saunas for about 5.6 million people, the world’s biggest coffee habit at roughly 12 kg a head, three-quarters forest and more metal bands per person than anywhere. That’s Finland. Sweden is a fair guess, but Sweden drinks less coffee and has far fewer saunas per person.
pearl: Finland was the first country in the world to elect women to parliament: 19 women won seats in 1907.

story: A spotty sprinter that would rather run than fight.

panels.name: Compared with a typical big cat

hints: That top speed is not normal for a cat.
A big cat that can’t roar and keeps its claws out, like running spikes.
why: The fastest land animal reaches about 100 km/h in short bursts, with strides of around 7 metres. Cheetahs can’t roar (they purr, chirp and yelp instead) and their claws stay partly out for grip, like a sprinter’s spikes. If you picked the lion, respect the confidence. The lion is still catching its breath.
pearl: A cheetah can only hold top speed for a few hundred metres before it overheats, so most chases are over in under a minute.

story: Flat, watery and very keen on two wheels.

panels.name: Compared with a typical European city

hints: Those bike numbers are doing a lot of work.
Plenty of water, but people live on it too.
why: About 100 km of canals, roughly a bike for every resident, and an estimated 12,000 to 15,000 bikes hauled out of the water every year. That’s Amsterdam. Venice has the canals but no bikes, and Copenhagen has the bikes but far fewer canals. Picked Venice? Lovely, but try cycling over a gondola.
pearl: Amsterdam’s canal ring was built in the 1600s and is UNESCO World Heritage listed. The city uses a special boat with a grabber to fish out the bikes.

story: Built for a fair, meant to be temporary, never left.

panels.name: Compared with a typical observation tower

hints: This tower is much older than most of its rivals.
Few towers pull this many visitors a year.
why: Opened in 1889 for the Paris World’s Fair, built from about 2.5 million rivets and puddle iron, repainted roughly every 7 years with about 60 tonnes of paint, and visited by around 6 million people a year. It’s the Eiffel Tower. Tokyo Tower is a cheeky guess: it’s 3 m taller but nearly 70 years younger.
pearl: It was meant to stand for only 20 years. It survived partly because it was useful as a giant radio antenna.

story: Tiny, shiny and running on sugar.

panels.name: Compared with a typical small bird

hints: Look at that daytime heart rate, then the night-time one.
Which bird can reverse out of a flower?
why: A heart rate over 1,200 bpm by day, falling to about 50 at night in a state called torpor, wings beating around 80 times a second, and the only birds that can truly fly backwards. It’s a hummingbird. Sunbirds look similar and also sip nectar, but they mostly perch to feed instead of hovering.
pearl: Hummingbirds live only in the Americas. Sunbirds fill the same nectar-drinking role in Africa, Asia and Australia.

story: Happy Halloween. Castles, forests and a certain famous count.

panels.name: Compared with its Eastern European neighbours
rows: Castle tied to the Dracula legend

hints: Its language is closer to Italian than to its neighbours’.
A gymnast scored a perfect 10 in 1976. And there’s that castle.
Castle tied to the Dracula legend
key: Castle tied to the Dracula legend
why: A Romance language in a mostly Slavic neighbourhood, at least 6,000 brown bears (over a third of Europe’s outside Russia), Bran Castle in Transylvania, and Nadia Comăneci, who at 14 scored the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics in 1976. It’s Romania. Picked Hungary? Spooky, but no castle with fangs.
pearl: The scoreboard at the 1976 Olympics couldn’t display 10.00, so Comăneci’s perfect score showed up as 1.00.
